title: Parish Finder by Coordinates: Civil Parishes
description: Look up a parish field when present in a reverse-geocoded address record.
summary_sentence: The result only reports a returned parish field. A missing field does not establish that no parish exists.
quick_answer: This tool reverse-geocodes the chosen point using Nominatim and displays available address fields from a nearby suitable mapped object. Fields may be missing or use broader fallbacks; the result is not a verified legal boundary or a guarantee of the nearest place.
steps_intro: The oldest layer of local government, one point at a time:

body.t: Parish councils hold the allotments, greens and benches. Knowing the parish routes the question to the right tiny council — the
Ancestors were baptised, married and buried by parish. A point's parish is the archive key for centuries of records.
Neighbourhood plans live at parish scale in England. The parish name frames which plan, which consultation, which meeting in the village hall.
Louisiana's counties are parishes — the record says so, and the finder reports the record. One word, two histories, both honoured.
Civil and ecclesiastical parishes diverged in the 19th century and now overlap imperfectly. The finder reports the record's parish; where both exist, the admin record usually means the civil one.
Much urban England is unparished — no parish council exists for the point. The finder says so plainly rather than adopting the nearest village's name.

faq: What if the answer says no parish?
The point is likely in an unparished area — common in larger towns and cities — or outside parish country. The finder reports the administrative record as it stands.
Is this the church parish?
Usually the record's parish is the civil one in England and Wales. Church parishes are a parallel geography; where the record holds that instead, it is what you see.
Can I use the tool without sharing my precise location?
Yes — type or click any point.
Why might a boundary or place name look different elsewhere?
Parish boundaries are ancient and occasionally revised; sources differ in vintage, and civil and church maps of the same name can diverge.
Does MapBench store my browser location?
No.
Parish or municipality?
In England the civil parish is the finer, older layer below district councils — the Municipality Finder reads the broader unit; this page reads the parish specifically.
Genealogy use?
A strong one — parish registers are organised by parish. Cross-check historic boundaries though: parishes moved less than counties, but they moved.
Louisiana addresses?
Enter the point; the record returns the parish (the county-equivalent) as Louisiana geography intends.
Welsh community councils?
Wales' equivalent tier is the community — the record's term is what the finder reports, Welsh geography in Welsh terms.
Parish councils versus parish meetings?
Smaller parishes may run a meeting rather than an elected council — the record's parish is the same geography either way; the governance detail lives with the county association.
Boundary stones and history?
Parish boundaries follow ancient lines — some along streams that have since moved. The record's line is the current administrative one; the history is a bonus layer for the curious.
